summary: On long missions, astronauts must spot health changes themselves because help from Earth is slow or delayed. Prana Watch is a health dashboard that gathers indicators across four NASA hazard areas: cabin air, radiation, isolation, and altered gravity. Each one gets a green, amber, or red status, and the most urgent one shows a clear checklist of what to do now. It has a Simulation mode with three 30-day mission scenarios, and a Live mode that measures the user's breathing through the microphone and accepts entered readings. CO2 and radiation limits come from NASA sources (NASA NTRS 20150019624, 20160014530; NASA-STD-3001). Simulation data is simulated; in flight, readings would come automatically from cabin sensors and wearables.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: Prana Watch is a health self-monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long-duration missions, where help from Earth is delayed or unavailable. It gathers health indicators across four NASA Human Research Program hazard areas (hostile closed environment, space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity), scores each one NOMINAL, CAUTION or WARNING, and turns the most urgent one into a step-by-step checklist the astronaut can act on immediately, without waiting for ground support.

HOW IT WORKS: The Cabin Air module is built on Tanmaatra, Neha's patent-pending breath biometric system (eCO2, TVOC and breath duration with a Random Forest classifier), retargeted from authentication to detecting CO2-exposure risk from breath. In Live mode the laptop microphone measures real breathing rate and exhale length; crew members also enter cabin CO2, radiation dose, heart rate, exercise, mood and sleep. Simulation mode replays three 30-day mission scenarios (nominal, CO2 scrubber failure, solar particle event). A mission selector (ISS, Artemis lunar surface, Mars transit) shows the Earth communication delay; on Mars, reports are queued for the flight surgeon and the crew is told to act on the checklist now. Thresholds come from NASA: the 180-day CO2 limit of 5.3 mmHg, ISS crew symptom reports from about 2.3 mmHg, and the 600 mSv career radiation limit with 250 mSv per solar particle event.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: Earlier detection of subtle problems (crews report CO2 symptoms well below official limits), faster action under comm delay, and one screen instead of scattered data. The same approach applies on Earth in submarines, polar stations and other closed environments.

TOOLS: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single offline file; Web Audio API for microphone breath detection; SVG charts and gauges. Hardware path: Tanmaatra eCO2/TVOC sensors with a Random Forest classifier.

CREATIVITY: Using breath as a health signal for spacecraft air quality, and designing around communication delay so the tool is built for autonomy.

FACTORS CONSIDERED: Autonomy under delayed communication, honesty about data (simulated data is clearly labelled; modules with no data show NO DATA instead of guessing), large touch targets and high contrast for use in flight, and a clear path from manual entry to automatic feeds from cabin sensors, dosimeters and wearables.
dataRefs: NASA HRP: Hazards of Human Spaceflight
CO2 on the ISS: An Operations Update (NTRS)
Health Risks of Reduced CO2 Exposures (NTRS)
projectRefs: CSA: Monitoring Radiation and Astronaut Health
CSA: Why Science Experiments in Space
